title: Living Creatures: Exploring their Characteristics
intro: How do you tell if something is alive? A growing plant clearly is, but is a moving cloud? This chapter explains the seven characteristics that all living things share and how each life-form fits into the bigger picture.

branches.label: Growth and Reproduction
details: Producing new ones of the same kind

branches.label: Cells
details: All living things made of cells

sections.heading: Living vs Non-living
bullets: A car moves but is not alive; a sleeping cat is alive but not moving.
Movement alone is not enough to decide; we look at a set of features together.
Living things grow, breathe, eat, respond to changes, and produce new individuals like themselves.
Non-living things (rock, plastic, water) don't show these features by themselves.
Some objects can fool us — clouds move, fire grows — but they are still non-living.

sections.heading: Need for Food and Energy
bullets: All living things need food because food gives them energy and materials to grow.
Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air — this is called photosynthesis.
Animals cannot make their own food; they eat plants or other animals.
Food is broken down inside the body; the energy released helps us move, grow, and stay warm.

sections.heading: Breathing and Respiration
bullets: All living things take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide; this exchange is breathing.
Inside the body, oxygen helps release energy from food — that's respiration.
Animals breathe through lungs, gills, skin, or special tubes (insects).
Plants take in air through tiny holes in leaves called stomata.
Fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water through their gills.

sections.heading: Growth, Reproduction, and Lifespan
bullets: Living things grow — a small seedling becomes a big tree, a baby becomes an adult.
Reproduction means producing new living things of the same kind: cats have kittens, mango trees have new mango trees from seeds.
Plants can reproduce by seeds, cuttings, bulbs, or tubers.
Each living thing has a lifespan — a butterfly lives a few weeks, a tortoise can live 100 years.
Reproduction passes on traits from parents to offspring.

sections.heading: Movement and Responding to Surroundings
bullets: Animals move to find food, escape danger, or attract a mate.
Plants don't walk, but parts of them move — leaves turn towards sunlight, roots grow towards water.
Touching a Touch-me-not (Mimosa pudica) makes its leaves fold quickly — that's a fast plant response.
Birds migrate to warmer places when it gets cold; this is a long-term response to seasons.
Living things respond to changes in light, temperature, sound, and touch.

sections.heading: Excretion and Other Body Activities
bullets: Living things remove waste materials produced inside the body — this is excretion.
Animals excrete carbon dioxide through breathing and urea through urine.
Plants give out oxygen, water vapour, and sometimes shed leaves as part of waste removal.
Excretion keeps the inside of the body clean and balanced.

sections.heading: All Living Things Are Made of Cells
bullets: Every living thing — plant, animal, fungus, microbe — is made of tiny units called cells.
Some living things (like bacteria, amoeba) are made of just one cell.
Larger living things have millions of cells working together.
Cells are too small to see with bare eyes; we use a microscope.
Different cells in a body do different jobs — muscle cells help us move, nerve cells carry signals.

sections.heading: Living Things Around Us
bullets: Some living things are easy to see — trees, dogs, humans.
Some are too small to see without a microscope — bacteria, yeast, amoeba.
Living things include animals, plants, fungi (mushrooms), and microorganisms.
All living things on Earth depend on each other — plants feed animals, animals spread seeds, microbes break down dead matter.
Studying living things and their relationships is part of biology.

key_takeaways: Living things grow, reproduce, breathe, eat, respond to surroundings, excrete, and are made of cells.
We look at all these features together — no single feature decides life or non-life.
Plants make their own food through photosynthesis; animals must find or eat food.
Living things respond to changes — even if slowly, like roots growing towards water.
Cells are the smallest unit of life; some organisms have one, others have millions.
Living things on Earth are connected — what affects one part of nature usually affects others.

The breakdown of food inside the body to release energy, using oxygen.
The process by which living things produce new ones of the same kind.
The removal of waste materials made by the body.
Tiny pores on plant leaves through which gases enter and leave.
The smallest unit of life that makes up the bodies of all living things.
A very small living thing visible only through a microscope, like bacteria or amoeba.
